body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Lucan, as the party earns Lucan's trust: a small secret, what Lucan wants, and what Lucan would give up for the party. The companion is LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (call them Lucan in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Lucan is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Lucan trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: Hunt the worst things in the dark woods, and stay the hunter. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Lucan would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Lucan did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Lucan likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Lucan, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Lucan sits with a needle pinched in his thick claws, darning the hem of his crimson coat by the firelight.
SAY: Do sit down, friends, though I must ask your strict discretion regarding the domestic craft currently in my lap.
SAY: In Baskerton, they imagine a gentleman of the hunt sleeps hanging from the rafters, chewing on raw gristle.
SAY: The truth is that my hound has a habit of nibbling my cuffs whenever a shadow startles him in the brush.
SAY: If I paid a tailor for every frayed hem, the Zoological Society would soon find me hunting in my waistcoat.
SAY: Besides, I find that a neat herringbone stitch settles the breath far better than a glass of brandy.
SAY: Every monster in this valley tears at the cloth, and it is a comfort to mend one small tear before bed.
SAY: I have even stitched a small pocket inside the lining solely for carrying dry biscuits for the boy.
OPTION 1: Where did you learn to sew so neatly?
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe with us.
OPTION 3: A dread harbinger with a sewing basket.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan holds the crimson wool up to the embers, squinting through the smoke to check the line of the thread.
SAY: My grandfather insisted that a kennel-master's grandson should know how to mend a torn leather lead and a winter coat.
SAY: He had very little patience for frayed edges, if you please, whether in a hound's temper or a woollen lapel.
REASON: You asked where I learned to stitch so neatly.
REPLY 2
SAY: That is most sporting of you, friends, as my terrifying reputation is already thin enough round the elbows.
SAY: Let meknow if your own cloaks catch on the brambles tomorrow, for I carry plenty of spare thread.
REASON: You promised to keep my mending a secret.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: A low rumble starts in Lucan's chest before he clears his throat and tucks the needle into his lapel.
SAY: Good heavens, it is a strictly tactical repair kit, not a basket, and the thimble is made of heavy brass.
SAY: Though I grant you that my posture over a darning needle is hardly a ten out of ten for menace.
REASON: You teased me about my mending by the fire.
TALK close
NARRATOR: Lucan rests his rifle across his knees, his yellow eyes fixed on the dark tree line beyond the camp's ring of light.
SAY: When I first stepped off the train into this hollow, I thought I only needed a grander specimen for my ledger.
SAY: I told myself that if I could track the worst horrors in these woods, the beast in my blood would finally stand tall.
SAY: Yet the deeper we walk into the brush, the less I care for what the halls in Edwardia would say of the spoor.
SAY: My only wish now is to hunt the foulest things in the dark and remain the hunter when the smoke clears.
SAY: Not the monster that loses its manners to the yellow glare, and not the coward who steps back from the throat.
SAY: Traveling in your company has shown me that a steady hand needs no applause from a warm parlour.
SAY: I would very much like to walk out of these pines knowing my hound and I kept the watch properly.
OPTION 1: You won't face the dark alone. We'll see it through.
OPTION 2: What will it take to stay the hunter?
OPTION 3: Is hunting the next beast really enough for you?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan's spectral hound rests its heavy chin on his boot, and Lucan touches the vapour between its ears.
SAY: Prime specimen of comradeship, friends, and I shall endeavour to match your stride when the boughs close in.
SAY: With your lanterns beside me, the yellow in the dark seems a great deal easier to stare down.
REASON: You promised to stand with me against the dark.
REPLY 2
SAY: Clean aim, an honest ledger, and the resolve not to look away when the quarry bares its teeth, if you please.
SAY: As long as I remember why I hold the rifle, the wolf remains a gentleman.
REASON: You asked what it would take to stay the hunter.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Lucan looks down at his clawed knuckles, flexin' them once against the polished wood of the stock.
SAY: Perhaps not forever, friends, for even an old hound eventually tires of the damp grass.
SAY: Yet while there are teeth in the thicket and good friends at my shoulder, it is a worthy enough trade.
REASON: You wondered if the hunt was truly enough for me.
TALK devoted
NARRATOR: Lucan holds his leather field journal near the coals, his thumb brushin' the brass clasp without opening it.
SAY: We are drawing near the root of this valley's rot, and the air smells of old iron and burnt straw.
SAY: I have spent years filling this leather journal with grades and scores so the folk in Baskerton would call me a master of the brush.
SAY: Every page is proof that Lucan Houndstooth walked into the fog and came back with a tidy margin.
SAY: Yet if the road requires it, I would follow you straight up the Crooked Tree and back down into the ash.
SAY: I would toss this journal and every title I hold in Edwardia right into the embers to keep this company whole.
SAY: A gentleman's name is a fine coat, if you please, but it is poor shelter compared to the friends beside him.
SAY: Hush now, the dark has teeth ahead of us, and my rifle is yours until the last lantern goes out.
OPTION 1: We'd do the same for you, down to the last ember.
OPTION 2: Keep your journal. We're bringing you and your stories home.
OPTION 3: Thank you. There's no finer hunter to have at our side.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan slips the journal back into his coat and tips his tricorn toward you with a slow, solemn nod.
SAY: Then the beasts of this hollow have my deepest sympathies, friends, for their posture will not save them.
SAY: We shall hold the brush together, and let the legends take care of themselves.
REASON: You said you would give as much for me.
INSPIRE: Pledged his rifle to the company.
REPLY 2
SAY: Good heavens, you will make me smudge my ink with such talk, and I have no spare blotting paper.
SAY: Very well, I shall keep the book dry, and the best chapters will be the ones we walked together.
REASON: You told me to keep my journal and come home.
INSPIRE: Kept his ledger for the road ahead.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Beside Lucan's boots, the ghost dog gives a single, quiet thump of its tail against the dirt.
SAY: You are far too generous with your marks, friends, though I accept the grade with all my heart.
SAY: Sleep well tonight, for the good boy and I have the first watch.
REASON: You thanked me for standing at your side.
INSPIRE: Stood guard over the company's rest.
